This model cube is the end result of the DYSMAL forward modeling process. The cube can now be used for comparisons and fitting to observed kinematic data, which we discuss in Section A.2.

A.2 Fitting Galaxy Kinematics using DYSMAL Models

The DYSMAL models presented in the previous subsection can be used to fit a wide variety of galaxy mass and kinematic components to a range of observational data.

First, a DYSMAL model set should be selected based on the specific application. For instance, this might be comprised of a disk, bulge, and halo mass components together with an intrinsic velocity dispersion profile, or it may include a galaxy disk together with an outflow component. The parameters of each of these model components are then set to a fixed value (e.g., fixed bulge-to-total ratio, B/TB/T), allowed to vary as free fit parameters (e.g., free total mass), or are determined as a function of some other parameter (e.g., fitting directly for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}), and then using this to find the halo mass for a NFW profile; alternatively, setting the halo mass from the total baryonic mass, using a fixed fgasf_{\mathrm{gas}} and a particular stellar mass-halo mass relation).

Next, depending on the type of observational data, extractions may need to be made from the DYSMAL model cubes. If the observations are to be fit in 3D, using IFS cubes, then the 3D mock DYSMAL cubes are directly comparable to the data. Alternatively, the models can be used to fit 2D extracted kinematic maps or 1D extracted kinematic profiles (or slit observations), for instance fitting both velocity VV and dispersion σ\sigma simultaneously (though other possibilities are to fit only VV, or to fit all of VV, σ\sigma, and the flux distribution). This is accomplished by applying the same extraction methodology used for the observations on the mock cubes (e.g., Gaussian-fit extractions to 2D velocity and dispersion maps; or flared or straight slit aperture extraction to 1D profiles).

We stress that all observational effects (including beam-smearing, the instrumental line spread function, and any extraction from 3D) are directly included in the resulting 1D/2D/3D DYSMAL models. The full forward modeling of this procedure therefore allows us to directly fit for the intrinsic model properties.

In DysmalPy, fitting can be performed either with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter space exploration (using emcee; Foreman-Mackey et al. 29) or least-squares fitting (using MPFIT; Markwardt 54). For MCMC fitting with emcee, priors log⁡p⁡(θi)\log p(\theta_{i}) are first selected for each free parameter θi\theta_{i} in the DYSMAL model; options include flat or Gaussian priors (either bounded or unbounded). The likelihood function for our model is defined to be a Gaussian distribution. For 3D fitting,

log⁡ℒ=\displaystyle\log\mathcal{L}= −0.5(1f)∑xsky,ysky,Vlosm(xsky,ysky,Vlos)×\displaystyle-0.5\left(\frac{1}{f}\right)\sum_{x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}}m(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})\ \times
\bBigg@3.5{\bBigg@3.5[Iobs​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)−Imod​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)errobs⁡(x,y,V)[w(xsky,ysky,Vlos)]−1/2\bBigg@3.5] 2\displaystyle\mathopen{\bBigg@}{3.5}\{\ \mathopen{\bBigg@}{3.5}[\frac{I_{\mathrm{obs}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})-I_{\mathrm{mod}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})}{\mathrm{err}_{{\mathrm{obs}}(x,y,V)}\left[w(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})\right]^{-1/2}}\mathclose{\bBigg@}{3.5}]^{\,2}
+log\bBigg@3.5[2​π​(errobs⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos))2w⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)\bBigg@3.5]\bBigg@3.5},\displaystyle\qquad+\log\ \mathopen{\bBigg@}{3.5}[\frac{2\pi\big(\mathrm{err}_{{\mathrm{obs}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})}\big)^{2}}{w(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})}\mathclose{\bBigg@}{3.5}]\ \mathclose{\bBigg@}{3.5}\}\,, (A14)

where ImodI_{\mathrm{mod}} is from Eq. A13, IobsI_{\mathrm{obs}} is the observed 3D cube, m⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)m(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}) is a data mask (e.g., removing bad pixels or low S/N regions), w⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)w(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}) is any weighting to be applied to the cube (e.g., effectively modifying the uncertainties), and ff is an optional factor to account for oversampling of the data relative to the spatial and spectral resolution of the data (to approximate the number of independent data points, removing any impact of oversampling on the relative importance of the likelihood and priors). For 2D or 1D fitting,

logℒ=−0.5(1f)×∑X=V,[σ],[flux]\displaystyle\log\mathcal{L}=-0.5\left(\frac{1}{f}\right)\times\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X=V,[\sigma],\\ \hskip 8.19447pt[\mathrm{flux}]\end{subarray}}
\bBigg@3.5{∑imi[wi(Xobs,i−Xmod,ierrX,i)2+log(2​π​errX,i2wi)]\bBigg@3.5},\displaystyle\mathopen{\bBigg@}{3.5}\{\sum_{i}m_{i}\left[w_{i}\left(\frac{X_{\mathrm{obs},i}-X_{\mathrm{mod},i}}{\mathrm{err}_{X,i}}\right)^{2}+\log\left(\frac{2\pi\ \mathrm{err}_{X,i}^{2}}{w_{i}}\right)\right]\mathclose{\bBigg@}{3.5}\}, (A15)

where XX is either the velocity VV, dispersion σ\sigma, or flux (e.g., 1D profiles along the slit V⁡(p)V(p), σ⁡(p)\sigma(p), I⁡(p)I(p), or 2D maps of VV, σ\sigma and line intensity II), and XobsX_{\mathrm{obs}} and XmodX_{\mathrm{mod}} are the data and extracted model maps/profiles, respectively. The outer sum over the maps/profiles XX includes only the maps/profiles that are being used for fitting (e.g., simultaneously fitting velocity VV and dispersion σ\sigma; see discussion above), and the sum over ii denotes the sum over all pixels or data points in the maps/profiles. Similar to the 3D log likelihood, mim_{i} is the data mask, wiw_{i} is any data weighting (or no weighting, with wi=1w_{i}=1), and ff is the optional factor accounting for spatial data oversampling. The log posterior probability is then

log⁡P⁡(θ|obs)=log⁡ℒ⁡(obs|θ)+log⁡p⁡(θ)+const,\log P(\theta|\mathrm{obs})=\log\mathcal{L}(\mathrm{obs}|\theta)+\log p(\theta)+\mathrm{const}, (A16)

with the log likelihood as defined above and taking the prior as the composite of the individual parameter priors, log⁡p⁡(θ)=∑ilog⁡p⁡(θi)\log p(\theta)=\sum_{i}\log p(\theta_{i}).

The “best-fit” parameter values are determined as the maximum a posteriori (MAP) values from the posteriors, with the option to jointly analyze the posteriors of parameters which exhibit degeneracies, to ensure the MAP values correspond to high probability regions of the multidimensional posterior distribution. The upper and lower 1​σ1\sigma uncertainties for each parameter are estimated independently, using the shortest 68% interval of the marginalized posterior (to ensure reasonable uncertainty estimates in cases where the marginalized posterior is peaked near a boundary for the parameter).

Alternatively, fitting can be performed with MPFIT, which uses the Levenberg-Marquardt technique to perform least-squares fitting. For the least-squares fitting with DysmalPy, we define χkin2\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{kin}} that is tailored to the data dimensionality. For 3D fitting,

χkin2=\displaystyle\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{kin}}= ∑xsky,ysky,Vlosm⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)​w​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)\displaystyle\sum_{x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}}m(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})\;w(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})
×[Iobs​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)−Imod​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)errIobs​(xsky,ysky,Vlos)]2\displaystyle\times\left[\frac{I_{\mathrm{obs}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})-I_{\mathrm{mod}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})}{\mathrm{err}_{I_{\mathrm{obs}}(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}})}}\right]^{2} (A17)

where as before, IobsI_{\mathrm{obs}} and ImodI_{\mathrm{mod}} are the observed and model 3D cubes, respectively, m⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)m(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}) is a mask based on the data (e.g., removing bad pixels or low S/N regions) and w⁡(xsky,ysky,Vlos)w(x_{\mathrm{sky}},y_{\mathrm{sky}},V_{\mathrm{los}}) is any weighting to be applied to the cube. For 2D or 1D fitting,

χkin2=∑X=V,[σ],[flux][∑imi​wi​(Xobs,i−Xmod,ierrX,i)2],\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{kin}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X=V,[\sigma],\\ \hskip 8.19447pt[\mathrm{flux}]\end{subarray}}\left[\sum_{i}m_{i}\,w_{i}\left(\frac{X_{\mathrm{obs},i}-X_{\mathrm{mod},i}}{\mathrm{err}_{X,i}}\right)^{2}\right], (A18)

where again XobsX_{\mathrm{obs}} and XmodX_{\mathrm{mod}} are the observed and model velocity, dispersion or flux maps/profiles (e.g., the observed V⁡(p)V(p), σ⁡(p)\sigma(p), and flux I⁡(p)I(p) along the slit for 1D profiles), the outer sum only includes the observed maps/profiles used for simultaneous fitting (e.g., both VV and σ\sigma, or all of VV, σ\sigma, and the flux distribution), and mim_{i} and wiw_{i} are the data mask and any weighting of the data, respectively.

The best-fit parameter values are then taken directly from the least-squares minimization solution. One approach to derive uncertainties for the least-squares fitting is to then sample the value of χkin2\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{kin}} over a grid of values for all free parameters, and use this to determine the uncertainty intervals. However, in practice it is often more computationally efficient to estimate the uncertainties through an accompanying MCMC exploration of the posterior distribution.

A.3 Importance of Prior Choice in MCMC Fitting

While MCMC fitting provides a number of benefits (e.g., simultaneously enabling uncertainty estimation), it is crucial to consider how the choice of priors impacts the sampled posterior distribution. In MCMC sampling, priors can help to restrict fits with degeneracies by applying constraints from ancillary information or physical feasibility (e.g., through bounding and/or the application of Gaussian priors), so that the posterior distribution reflects both the likelihood from the data and these prior constraints. Parameter priors can also be uniform, so the posterior is driven by the likelihood function. However, even adopting uniform priors is a choice that impacts later analysis, because the sampled posterior distribution also depends on how the fit was parameterized.77 7 For further discussion on the impact of parameter transformations on probability (i.e., prior and posterior) distributions, see Sivia & Skilling [73], Hogg [47], and Hogg & Foreman-Mackey [48].

The impact of priors is particularly important when analyzing parameters inferred from the fit values. While not fit directly, there is an “effective prior” imprinted on the distribution of sample values for these derived parameters. This “effective prior” is determined by the choice of free fit parameters and their chosen priors (even uniform priors), and depends on the relationship between the fit and derived parameters. Formally, this is simply a change of variables in a probability distribution function (pdf), going from the fit parameter’s prior pdf to a transformed pdf. If xx and yy are related through y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) and xx is fit with a uniform, bounded prior, then as the total probability must be conserved,88 8 I.e., ∫abpX​(x)​𝑑x=∫f⁡(a)f⁡(b)pY​(y)​𝑑y\int_{a}^{b}p_{X}(x)\,dx=\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}p_{Y}(y)\,dy the effective prior on yy will be proportional to |dd​y​[f−1​(y)]|\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\frac{d}{dy}\left[f^{-1}(y)\right]\right\rvert}, where f−1f^{-1} is the inverse function (Casella & Berger 12, Eq. 2.1.10).99 9 More generally, for a prior pdf pX​(x)p_{X}(x) for xx, the transformed prior pdf for y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) is pY​(y)=pX​(f−1​(y))​|dd​y​[f−1​(y)]|p_{Y}(y)=p_{X}\left(f^{-1}(y)\right)\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\frac{d}{dy}\left[f^{-1}(y)\right]\right\rvert}, assuming “well-behaved” functions (i.e., pX​(x)p_{X}(x) is continuous and normalizable, and f−1​(y)f^{-1}(y) is continuously differentiable; Casella & Berger 12, Sec 2.1, Theorem 2.1.5).

The issue of free parameter and prior selection can have a large impact when fitting galaxy kinematics using MCMC sampling with DysmalPy. For example, for a fit with a baryonic component and a NFW halo, if log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}) is chosen as the free parameter with a flat prior, then the distribution of fDM​(Re)=vDM2​(Re)/vcirc2​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})=v_{\mathrm{DM}}^{2}(R_{e})/v_{\mathrm{circ}}^{2}(R_{e}) for the MCMC sampling (calculated as “blobs” from the emcee sampler) will often diverge towards 0 and 1. This arises in part because a flat prior on log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}) is equivalent to a prior for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) that diverges as fDM​(Re)→0f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})\to 0, or fDM​(Re)→1f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})\to 1, because sampling uniformly from the log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}) prior produces a pile-up of log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}) values that all map to similarly small/large values of fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}). If fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) is fairly poorly constrained by the data (i.e., a shallow likelihood function), the effective probability distribution for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) will thus primarily reflect this “effective,” diverging prior.

Therefore, if the aim is to measure fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) rather than log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}), it is better to fit directly for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}). For this inverted parameterization, the choice of a flat prior for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) corresponds to an effective prior on log10⁡(Mvir/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{vir}}/M_{\odot}) that is a peaked distribution (i.e., essentially the inverse of the opposite case that diverges towards the bounds). Because of this parameterization and prior choice issue, in this paper we chose to fit directly for fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}), as this is the quantity of interest.

A.4 DYSMAL Parameter Fitting Degeneracies for
RC41 Curves and the Impact of Priors

Fitting the kinematics of high-redshift galaxies with mass and kinematic models --- such as with DYSMAL --- is complicated by degeneracies between different components. These degeneracies arise in part from the impact of beam smearing, given the relatively low spatial resolution of the observations, and from relatively modest S/N of the data, even for very deep observations such as our RC41 sample. At lower S/N and lower spatial resolution, it can be difficult to disentangle the velocity signatures of a bulge, thick disk, and halo, as profile differences can be smoothed out to the point where they cannot be distinguished within the observational uncertainties.1010 10 We note that while we focus here on how these issues impact parametric kinematic modeling, these resolution and S/N limitations of the data also complicate constraints of galaxy kinematics using nonparametric methods. Thus, while the lower halo concentrations at higher redshifts should help to break the disk-halo degeneracy that is observed in local galaxies (see the discussion in 44), the relatively limited spatial resolution and S/N of our observations compared to what is currently achievable for local galaxies tends to produce a similar baryon-halo degeneracy.

When modeling our galaxies with a bulge, a thick disk, a NFW halo, and a constant intrinsic velocity dispersion (with free parameters log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}), fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}), Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}, and σ0\sigma_{0}), we tend to find an anti-correlation between the total baryonic mass and the dark matter fractions. This degeneracy is not unexpected, as it roughly traces lines of constant vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}, reflecting a trade-off between dark and baryonic matter that is accentuated by the smoothing of the different velocity curve shapes by the effects of beam smearing (i.e., the total mass is better constrained than the mass partitioning). However, the exact position and shape of this degeneracy depends on the values of other model parameters, particularly the intrinsic velocity dispersion σ0\sigma_{0} and the disk effective radius, Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}.

The values of σ0\sigma_{0} and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} are connected to the dark matter fraction–baryonic mass degeneracy through the asymmetric drift correction (see Sec. VI.2) and both the definition fDM​(Re≡Re,disk)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}\equiv R_{e,\mathrm{disk}}) and the role of Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} in setting the model rotation curve profile, respectively. In general, increasing both σ0\sigma_{0} and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} results in shifting the region of highest fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})–log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) likelihood towards lines of higher vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}, as illustrated in the left panel of Figure 7. Increasing σ0\sigma_{0} leads to larger asymmetric drift corrections, or lower vrotv_{\mathrm{rot}} for a fixed model vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}} (i.e., fixed total mass). Matching the observed vrotv_{\mathrm{rot}} thus requires increasing vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}. When increasing Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}, the intrinsic rotation curve profile is stretched to peak/flatten at larger radii, without impacting the maximum rotation velocity. Therefore, to match the inner rising profile of the observed vrot​(r)v_{\mathrm{rot}}(r), the total mass must also be increased (i.e., higher model vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}). The exact position and extent of this degeneracy is more complex than this fixed-value illustration, as all four parameters (log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}), fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}), Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}, σ0\sigma_{0}) are free. Nonetheless, this simplified picture helps to understand the likelihood degeneracy for the full fit, as a range of σ0\sigma_{0} or Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} values will contribute to a broadening of the degeneracy region (i.e., spanning more values of vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}), roughly corresponding to overlapping regions of fixed σ0\sigma_{0} and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}.

The final posterior degeneracy between fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}) and log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) depends not only on the likelihood degeneracy, but also on the Gaussian priors on log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}}. In the limit where the data are not highly informative, the Gaussian priors will help to restrict the posteriors of these parameters to narrower ranges. Thus, the log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) prior will help break the fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})–log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) degeneracy by “picking out” a subsection of the log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) values covered (see Figure 7, right panel). The Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} prior will also have an impact, since a narrowing of the Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} parameter space will translate to narrowing of the diagonal shift of the fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})–log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) anti-correlation (effectively, fewer overlapping degeneracy regions, as fewer Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} values are highly probable).

To illustrate the parameter degeneracies and the role of the priors, in Figure 8 we show the prior, likelihood, and posterior distributions in all 1D and 2D projected spaces for one galaxy in our sample (BX482). The posterior distribution (black lines and black/grey filled regions) is determined from the 1D MCMC sampler chain, and the likelihood distribution (orange lines and contours) is approximated by performing a separate MCMC sampling with uninformative (i.e., bounded flat) priors for all parameters.1111 11 Technically, this gives a posterior distribution that is directly proportional to the likelihood. However, as we are concerned with relative distributions for this illustration, this is an acceptable approximation. See Hogg & Foreman-Mackey [48] for an in-depth discussion on MCMC sampling and prior, likelihood, and posterior distributions. The 1D priors are shown with dotted blue lines, and the center and standard deviation of the Gaussian priors on log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} are marked with blue lines and shaded regions in the projected 1D and 2D panels, and the 1D histograms are all normalized, as the correct scaling factors have not been determined.

The impact of the Gaussian priors on log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) and Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} can be seen in both the 1D and 2D histograms, as the posterior peaks for these parameters lie between the prior and likelihood peaks (as do the MAP values, which are found by jointly analyzing all free parameters; white plus signs), and the marginalized posterior distribution peaks are less broad than those of the likelihood. Because of the fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e})–log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) degeneracy (bottom left panel), the log10⁡(Mbar/M⊙)\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{bar}}/M_{\odot}) prior also impacts the posterior distribution of fDM​(Re)f_{\mathrm{DM}}(R_{e}), and yields a narrower posterior degeneracy than for the likelihood distribution. The restriction of the Re,diskR_{e,\mathrm{disk}} values from the prior also contributes to narrowing of the degeneracy region, but in the direction perpendicular to the anti-correlation (i.e., spanning a narrower range of constant vcircv_{\mathrm{circ}}; see Figure 7). Although the actual posterior probability distributions for each galaxy will also depend on other model parameters and on the peculiarities of the observed rotation and dispersion curves, the trends discussed here account for the overall qualitative properties of the posteriors determined from our MCMC analysis of the RC41 sample.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
